---
title: "Try it locally"
---

You can run the entire platform against a disposable OMERO server on your own
machine — no institutional server, no credentials, no data of your own. This is
the fastest way to see what OMERO-Screen actually does.

::: {.callout-note}
Allow about 30 minutes end to end, most of which is the first Docker pull and
the Cellpose model download.
:::

## What you need

- **Docker**, running. The test server is a container pair (OMERO + Postgres).
- **Python 3.12** and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), as in
  [Install & configure](installation.qmd).
- **A GPU helps but is not required.** On CPU, segmentation is slow but works —
  the sample plate is deliberately small.

## 1. Start the test server

```bash
./scripts/manage_test_server.sh start
```

This brings up `docker-compose.test.yml` and waits for OMERO to accept
connections on port 4064. It is a throwaway instance: `stop` shuts it down,
and the data lives in a Docker volume you can delete.

```bash
./scripts/manage_test_server.sh status    # is it up?
./scripts/manage_test_server.sh stop      # shut it down
```

Point your environment at it by setting `ENV=e2etest`, which loads
`.env.e2etest` — that file already contains the container's credentials
(`root` / `omero` on `localhost`), so nothing needs editing.

```bash
export ENV=e2etest
uv run omero-integration-test e2e_connection
```

A clean run confirms the server is up and the client can authenticate.

### 2b. Using your own data

`load_plates.sh` imports Operetta-layout plates — directories containing
`*/Images/Index.idx.xml` — into a project named "Screens".

```bash
./scripts/load_plates.sh                        # show the options
./scripts/load_plates.sh -d /path/to/plates -x  # -x actually executes
```

Note the plate ID it reports; every command below takes it.

## 3. Run the pipeline

```bash
uv run omero-screen <plate_id>
```

Metadata is parsed, flatfield masks are built, every well is segmented with
Cellpose, features are extracted, and — if an EdU channel is present — each
cell is assigned a cell-cycle phase. Results are attached back to the plate as
CSVs, with QC figures alongside.

Add `--stitch` to segment each well as a single canvas instead of field by
field. See [Your first plate](first-plate.qmd) for what each stage does.

## 4. Inspect the segmentation

```bash
uv run napari
```

Open the **Welldata Widget** from the plugin menu, enter the plate ID, and step
through wells to see the segmentation overlaid on the raw channels. This is the
quickest way to judge whether the masks are sensible. The
[napari guide](../../napari/) covers the other widgets.

## 5. Import into the database

```bash
uv run cellview import plate <plate_id>
uv run cellview plate <plate_id>      # summary, conditions, measurement counts
uv run cellview projects              # everything in the database
```

## 6. Make a figure

```python
from cellview.api import cellview_load_data
from omero_screen_plots import cellcycle_plot, save_fig

df, conditions = cellview_load_data(<plate_id>)
fig, ax = cellcycle_plot(df, conditions=conditions)
save_fig(fig, "cell-cycle")
```

The [plots documentation](../../plots/) covers the other plot types and the
statistics behind them.

## 7. Optional: train a classifier

If you want to exercise the machine-learning path, generate labelled crops
from the napari training widget, then:

```bash
uv run cellclass dataset <crops_dir> --name demo --channels DAPI Tub
uv run cellclass train demo.npz --epochs 50 --no-wandb
```

The [CellClass guide](../../cellclass/) explains the architecture sweep and
the metrics.

## Cleaning up

```bash
./scripts/manage_test_server.sh stop
docker volume prune          # removes the throwaway OMERO data
```

## If something fails

| Symptom | Usually means |
|---|---|
| `Connection refused` on 4064 | The container is still starting; wait and re-run `status` |
| Authentication error | `ENV=e2etest` is not exported, so a different `.env` was loaded |
| "No metadata found" | The plate has no Excel attachment and no map-annotations |
| Segmentation extremely slow | Running on CPU — expected; use a smaller plate |
